clinicalPearls: A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive injury or malformation of the developing brain, though the clinical picture can change as the child grows.
It is the most common cause of chronic motor disability beginning in childhood.
Classified by motor type (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, or mixed) and by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia).
Spastic forms are most common; early signs include abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, delayed motor milestones, and early hand preference before one year.
Preterm birth, low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic injury, infection, kernicterus, and brain malformations are recognised risk factors.

Frequent comorbidities include intellectual disability, epilepsy, visual and hearing impairment, feeding and swallowing difficulties, communication problems, and orthopaedic complications such as hip subluxation and contractures.
Diagnosis is largely clinical; MRI often identifies the underlying lesion and helps establish aetiology.
Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, aiming to maximise function and participation with therapy, orthotics, spasticity treatment, and orthopaedic care rather than cure.
Because the disorder is static, clear progression or regression of neurological signs should prompt a search for an alternative, evolving diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Cerebral palsy results from injury or maldevelopment of the immature brain from any of a range of prenatal, perinatal, or early postnatal insults. In preterm infants, periventricular white-matter injury (periventricular leukomalacia) commonly affects descending motor tracts, producing spastic diplegia; in term infants, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, malformations, stroke, or kernicterus may be responsible. The primary lesion is non-progressive, but secondary musculoskeletal changes such as contractures and bony deformity evolve over time.
additionalDifferentials: Spinal muscular atrophy and other neuromuscular disorders
Global developmental delay without a motor disorder
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to identify structural or ischaemic lesions
Metabolic or genetic testing if the presentation is atypical or progressive
Hip surveillance imaging to detect subluxation
Evaluation of feeding, swallowing, and nutrition
redFlags: Loss of previously acquired skills or clear neurological progression (suggests an alternative diagnosis)
Signs of aspiration or faltering growth from feeding difficulty
Rapidly increasing spasticity or dystonia causing pain or care difficulty
reference.prognosis: The motor impairment itself is non-progressive, and life expectancy is often near normal in milder forms; outcome depends on severity, mobility level, and comorbidities, with severe quadriplegia, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and feeding problems associated with greater disability and shorter survival.
pitfalls: Labelling a child with cerebral palsy when the course is actually progressive (missing a treatable metabolic or genetic disorder)
Focusing only on motor impairment and overlooking epilepsy, sensory, or feeding comorbidities
Neglecting hip surveillance, allowing silent dislocation
Underestimating cognition in non-verbal children with good comprehension
management: Coordinate multidisciplinary supportive care for the non-progressive lesion, centred on physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maximise function
Manage spasticity with oral agents such as baclofen, focal botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen or selective dorsal rhizotomy
Undertake orthopaedic surveillance with hip surveillance imaging and corrective surgery for subluxation and contractures
Treat comorbid epilepsy with antiseizure medication
Address feeding and swallowing difficulties with speech and language assessment and gastrostomy for nutrition, and treat drooling
Assess and manage visual, hearing, communication and intellectual impairments, including augmentative communication
Provide orthoses, mobility aids and assistive technology, with family support and planned transition to adult services
